read.bigIdea: Four kinds of malt build every beer.
read.where: Cicerone groups malt into **kilned base** malts (**Pils**, **pale**, **Vienna**, **Munich**), **kilned specialty** malts (biscuit, Victory), **crystal or caramel** malts and **roasted** malts. **Crystal** malt is “stewed” wet so its starch turns to sugar inside the husk: it adds **caramel**, color and **body**. **Roasted** malts (chocolate, black) add **coffee** and **chocolate**. **Roasted barley** isn’t malted at all: it’s raw barley roasted like coffee, and it gives Irish stout its bitter coffee edge.
read.mixup: Munich and Vienna malts are base malts: they can be most of the beer, not just a pinch.

read.bigIdea: A hop tastes of where it grows.
read.where: **“Noble” hops** is a 1980s marketing term for four old Central European aroma hops: **Hallertau**, **Spalt**, **Tettnang** and **Saaz** (from Žatec, the hop of Czech pilsner). England’s classics are **East Kent Golding** (earthy, apricot) and **Fuggle**. America’s **Cascade** (1971) is floral and **grapefruit**; **Citra** is citrus, tropical, lychee; **Mosaic** is blueberry and tangerine. New Zealand’s **Nelson Sauvin** is named for its likeness to Sauvignon Blanc; Australia’s **Galaxy** is passion fruit and peach.
read.mixup: “Noble” isn’t a quality rating. It’s a name for four traditional hops.
read.sayIt: It’s hopped with Citra, so it’s tropical and citrusy.

keyPoints.line: where most people start tasting it.

read.bigIdea: IBU measures bitterness, not how bitter it tastes.
read.where: Hop bitterness comes from **alpha acids**, which barely dissolve until the **boil** turns them into **iso-alpha acids**: the longer a hop boils, the more bitterness it gives. One **IBU** is about **1 mg/L** of iso-alpha acids. Most people start tasting bitterness around **4–9 IBU**, and the practical ceiling is about **110**. Malt **sweetness** and body **mask** bitterness, so two beers with the same IBU can taste very different.
read.mixup: A 60 IBU imperial stout can taste less bitter than a 40 IBU pale ale: the malt hides it.

keyPoints.line: high sulfate: dry, bitter pale ale.

read.where: **Pilsen**’s water is very **soft**, part of why the first pilsner (1842) stood out. **Burton-on-Trent**’s well water is full of **gypsum** (calcium sulfate), which gives pale ales and IPAs a **dry, crisp** bitterness; brewers copy it by “Burtonizing”. Water high in **carbonate**, as in **Dublin**, **London** and **Munich**, balances the acidity of dark malts, which is why those cities became known for **porter, stout** and **dark lager**. Chlorine must be removed, or it makes medicinal flavors.
read.mixup: Hard water isn’t one thing: sulfate and carbonate do very different jobs.

keyPoints.line: Weizen = banana and clove; Brett = funk.

read.where: **Weizen** yeast makes **banana** (isoamyl acetate) and **clove** (4-vinylguaiacol); many **Belgian** yeasts make spicy phenols. **Brettanomyces** is a wild yeast with a **farmyard** funk that also dries beer out. **Candi sugar** ferments completely, so it raises alcohol while keeping the beer **light and dry**: why a tripel drinks easier than its strength. **Lactose** doesn’t ferment and stays sweet (sweet stout). **Pasteurization** heats beer to stop spoilage: pasteurized draft keeps about **90–120 days**, unpasteurized about **45–60**.
read.mixup: Sugar in a Belgian beer makes it drier, not sweeter: the yeast eats it all.
